transcript.text: Good morning and welcome to City Football Club.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’d like to give you some useful information about your visit to the stadium today and then we’ll start the tour of the areas of the stadium that are open to visitors.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I can see lots of children here today, so just to let mums and dads know a few things before we start.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The stadium has lots of stairs and the players’ tunnel is very dark.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Please don’t let your children wander off on their own, even for a minute.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We don’t want any accidents or anyone getting frightened.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Cameras are permitted everywhere and you can take pictures of your child shooting a penalty.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Assistants are helping to organise this and hopefully the queue won’t be too long.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s very hot and sunny out on the pitch today.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You can get food and drink at the cafe and I really recommend the healthy lunch boxes for children Also in the cafe, children are invited to do a football drawing.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We pick the best one at the end of the afternoon.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So don’t forget to put your name and contact details on the back.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That way if you’ve left the stadium before then, we’ll send your prize, but sadly we can’t return drawings.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’d like to mention some features of the tour.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ll start with the 360 cinema experience, which has been very popular over the years, and then I’ll take you to the players’ dressing rooms, before going outside to the seating area and the pitch.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I should say, if you’d prefer your visit to be self-guided, please collect headphones from the reception, and then you can listen to the pre-recorded information at your own speed.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve only just introduced this feature and would appreciate your feedback.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’re thinking of offering tours in other languages in future, so if you have any thoughts on that, we’d welcome those too.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you plan to return another time, you might like to book one of our VIP tours.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve only just started offering these and they can be booked online.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now, the stadium you see today was built in 1989 as part of a three-year redevelopment project.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: While that project was going on, the team had to play its matches at the ground of another club.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Apart from that, the club has been here on this site since 1870.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As some of you may know, that was the start of a really important decade in the history of football in this country.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: For example, 1870 was also the year that football teams started to include a player whose role it was to guard the goal.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s hard to imagine what the game must have been like without someone in that position, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In 1872 and 73, many other clubs were established, both here and abroad.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And the following year, in 1874, referees were allowed to send players off if they committed certain offences.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And also in that year, teams started having to swap ends at half-time.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One fact I was interested to discover was that in early football games the aim was for the scorer to get the ball between two flag posts and later between sticks joined at the top with a piece of tape.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In 1875, that tape was replaced with the solid crossbar that we’re familiar with today. 1877 saw the founding of further new clubs and the history books tell us that in the same year all the clubs decided to set a limit of 90 minutes for each match Before that it was a more casual arrangement and this sometimes caused huge arguments and sometimes fights during matches when one team called the end of the game and the other team wanted to play on to try and score a winning goal.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: By 1878, the number of teams in the Football League increased again.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In addition, referees started using whistles and electric lamps were installed on certain pitches.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This was a significant change, as games could then be played in the evenings all year round.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In 1880, clubs began to charge fans for admission to games, even though players were still amateurs and had other proper jobs.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s hard to imagine in the modern professional game. where top players earn significant sums of money from both playing and commercial activities.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve been looking at different types of conflicts that may arise between wildlife and humans at the boundaries of protected areas, such as national parks and animal sanctuaries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I’d like to illustrate this by telling you about some research that I’ve been involved in recently in the Central African country of Zambia in the area around the Chembe Bird Sanctuary which contains over 300 of the listed birds of Zambia These include a number of birds of prey such as eagles hawks and owls that live by hunting and killing other birds and animals Now most of the people living in the local communities near to the bird sanctuary are small-scale farmers and these birds of prey provide important social and ecological benefits to them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, a lot of damage can be caused to farmers’ crops by rodents, such as rats, which would consume the crops as they grow in the fields, as well as after harvesting if they weren’t hunted and killed by the birds.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And the predatory habits of these birds also protect farmers in other ways.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal, and birds of prey have a major role in keeping their populations under control.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Local people have always been aware of these benefits and for years, even before the sanctuary was opened in 1973, the birds played a key role in the culture of the region.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, more recently, the sanctuary and its birds have also become increasingly important to the community in economic terms, because at present, after a relatively slow start, tourism has become an important source of revenue for them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, although these birds of prey are protected by the government, their numbers are falling.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some of these deaths are accidental.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Fatalities occur when birds alight on roads to catch and eat their prey, and are hit by fast moving traffic.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Drivers in Zambia have to take special care at night, as birds may regard the quieter roads as safe places to sleep.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Accidental deaths may also occur if these birds fly close to high power lines as they may be electrocuted.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is a particular danger in the heavy rain which can occur in the region in the months from December to April.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And local farmers also pose a threat to these birds.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As well as growing crops, small-scale farmers in the area also rear chickens.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These provide food for the farmers’ families, as well as being an important source of income.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But they’re also an easy target for birds of prey, and so farmers may shoot these birds, which is illegal but understandable, or they may poison the birds, which again is illegal and can have negative effects on the ecosystem.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So how else can farmers protect their chickens from birds of prey?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some people believe that to prevent the predators from settling near the area where the chickens are kept, it’s best to keep this area free from vegetation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But in fact, this is counterproductive, as it means the chickens have no cover to hide in and they’ll be easier for the birds to see.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another possibility would be to prevent the chickens from going outside at all and to keep them safe from predators inside a building, but this would cost far too much to be a practical solution.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Nearly all the farmers reported that they spent a lot of time and effort trying to frighten off the birds of prey without actually harming them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Most of the farmers had at least one dog and said this was a big help at scaring away the predators.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some of the farmers also reported that during the breeding season, when the chickens were particularly vulnerable, they encouraged their children to watch over the chickens and to hit pans with a metal spoon so that the resulting noise would succeed in driving away birds that were trying to seize the young chicks None of these methods was 100% effective so as a result the village people told us that rather than just using one method, they were forced to use a combination for them to have any effect.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And even so, these birds of prey remain a major threat to the chickens’ survival and cause considerable economic loss to farmers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So we looked at the possibility of a longer-term solution to…
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
